newsitem.title: UK: Veggies fight heart disease, cancer, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Veggies fight heart disease, cancer, study finds.

text.p: Eating a few extra pieces of fruit or vegetables a day can put enough vitamins into circulation to protect against heart disease and cancer, researchers in New Zealand reported on Friday.
They found volunteers who ate extra servings of fruit and vegetables dramatically increased the levels of vitamins in their blood.

Jim Mann and colleagues at the University of Otago in Dunedin noted that people have been urged to increase their intake of vitamins like A, C and E because of studies showing their antioxidant effects -- neutralising damage that can lead to heart disease and cancer

"A common response to these recommendations has been a dramatic increase in the consumption of antioxidant supplements, despite little evidence of benefit," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
They decided to test the effects of eating fruit and vegetables.
They tested the blood of 87 volunteers who had normal cholesterol levels and who normally ate three or fewer servings of fruit and vegetables a day.

Half the patients stayed on their regular diet while half were told to eat eight servings of fruit and vegetables a day. "They were given detailed dietary instructions, menu suggestions and recipes, reinforced during fortnightly individual interviews," Mann's group wrote.
A serving equalled half a cup of cooked vegetables, a medium-sized piece of fruit or 3/4 of a cup of vegetable juice.

They found "striking differences" between the two groups in blood levels of vitamin C as well as vitamin A precursors alpha and beta carotene. The group that ate more fruit and vegetables had higher levels.
"On the basis of comparison with epidemiological data, the concentrations of plasma antioxidants achieved might be expected to reduce the risk of cancer," Mann's team wrote.
"At least 10 prospective studies have shown that high intakes of fruit and vegetables confer protection against cancer, cardiovascular disease and stroke."
Several other studies have indicated that it is not possible to fudge by taking supplements --people who take vitamin pills do not seem to enjoy the same benefits.
The volunteers showed little change in levels of vitamin E, however, and it could be people needed extra advice on where to get E, which is found in vegetable fats and nuts.
